newsitem.title: INDIA: Decentralisation could drive India reform - Economist.
newsitem.headline: Decentralisation could drive India reform - Economist.

text.p: A trend towards increasing economic and political decentralisation could drive India's second stage of radical reform, Britain's Economist magazine said on Friday.
A special report on India will appear in the February 22 issue of the magazine, an advance copy of which was given to Reuters.
It said Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda's ruling coalition is too fragile to successfully meet the challenges that must be surmounted to avoid falling behind other developing nations.
It called for the pace of economic reforms, which began pulling down the decades-old walls of a socialist economy in 1991, to be accelerated.

"Though India is changing faster than at any time since British rule came to an end, the government must accelerate the pace of reform to avoid falling further behind other developing nations, especially the East Asian Tigers," it said.
Reforms have pushed the country's growth rate from four percent a year between 1960 and 1990 to roughly seven percent a year since 1994, the magazine said in a statement that accompanied the report.
"India's reformers still have a great deal to do before the task begun in 1991 is complete," it warned.
The survey found many public sector enterprises as well as private sector businesses still remain protected against competition, though India's markets have opened to competition.

Though India has reduced its weighted average import tariff to 27 percent from the 1991 level of 87 percent, the figure is still twice as high as the average in most of East Asia and Latin America, The Economist said.
In foreign direct investment (FDI), it said, India appears at first glance to be making great progress.
India received nearly $2 billion of FDI in 1995 -- a handsome increase over 1991's $150 million but only a fraction of the $38 billion FDI China received in 1995.
"The reason for this, as foreign investors unanimously complain, is that the system simply does not work as it is supposed to," The Economist said.

"India's future depends on radical reform, strong political leadership and a willingness by government to confine its role in the economy to those few crucial areas where free enterprise alone is not enough," the magazine said.
"However, the ruling coalition -- an ill-matched grouping of 13 different parties is too fragile to meet these challenges."
But the survey discerned signs that decentralisation could ultimately drive India's second stage of radical reform.

"If states gain more control of their own economic destinies reform-minded state governments could become pioneers of liberalisation, promoting competition between states that would in turn promote further reform," The Economist concluded.
